entities.summary: Ehremar or Ebramar or Evremar was a Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1102 to 1105 or 1107, and then Archbishop of Caesarea. He was a prominent figure in the Latin Church during the 12th century, playing a key role in the politics of the Holy Land. His tenure as Patriarch was marked by controversy and power struggles with the local Christian communities. He was succeeded by his brother, Evremar, who also held the position of Patriarch. Ehremar's legacy as a leader in the Latin Church has been the subject of ongoing historical debate and analysis. The city of Caesarea, where he served as Archbishop, was an important center of Christian learning and culture during this period. The legacy of Ehremar continues to be felt in the modern-day Christian communities of the Middle East. The impact of his leadership on the politics of the Holy Land has been studied by historians for its insights into the complex relationships between Christian and Muslim communities in the region. Ehremar's story serves as a reminder of the enduring importance of the Latin Church in the history of Christianity.

Born in Thérouanne, Ponthieu, France around 1100, he was of Frankish noble descent. His tenure as Patriarch was marked by the establishment of the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem in 1102, which aimed to promote Christian influence in the region. Ebremaro di Thérouanne played a crucial role in the First Crusade, participating in the Siege of Antioch in 1097-1098. He was succeeded by Anselm of Havelock as Patriarch of Jerusalem in 1105. Ebremaro di Thérouanne also served as Archbishop of Caesarea, where he oversaw the construction of several churches and monasteries. His legacy as a prominent figure in the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem has endured, with his name becoming synonymous with the institution. Despite his significant contributions to the region, Ebremaro di Thérouanne's life and legacy are not as well-documented as those of his contemporaries, leaving room for further historical investigation.
